language.name: Ancient Greek
language.coverageNote: Starter study lexicon (70 authored words) plus 960 core lemmas from Major's 80% list and high-frequency LXX/New Testament vocabulary. Every inflectable entry carries three attested forms with different case/number, gender, or tense/voice/mood, and three different sentence patterns.

examples.translation: The word is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the word.

examples.original: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
examples.translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
examples.author: The Gospel according to John

entries.etymology: Derived from λέγω 'gather, say'; the noun denotes a collected account, speech, or reasoned statement.

examples.translation: The human being is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the human being.
Of all things the measure is man.
examples.author: Protagoras (as quoted by Plato)

entries.etymology: Compound of ἀνήρ 'man' and ὤψ 'face, appearance' is traditionally suggested, though the derivation is disputed.
entries.etymologyNote: The etymology is debated; the compound analysis is conventional rather than certain.

examples.translation: The god is good.
The god is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the god.

entries.etymology: Of uncertain origin; the word is not securely connected to any single Indo-European root.

examples.translation: The beginning is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the beginning.
In the beginning was the Word.
examples.author: The Gospel according to John

entries.etymology: From ἄρχω 'begin, rule'; the noun means both 'beginning' and 'rule, office'.

examples.translation: The soul is immortal.
The soul is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the soul.

entries.etymology: From ψύχω 'breathe, blow'; the noun originally denotes breath and then the life or soul.

examples.translation: The city is great.
The city is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the city.

entries.etymology: Etymology debated; the word is not securely derived from a single Indo-European root.

examples.translation: The man is wise.
The man is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the man.

entries.etymology: From PIE *h₂nḗr 'man'; the stem ἀνδρ- appears outside the nominative singular.

examples.translation: The woman is beautiful.
The woman is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the woman.

entries.etymology: From PIE *gʷḗn 'woman'; English 'queen' is related through Germanic.

examples.translation: The father loves his son.
The father is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the father.

entries.etymology: From PIE *ph₂tḗr 'father'; Latin pater and English 'father' are cognates.

examples.translation: The mother loves her daughter.
The mother is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the mother.

entries.etymology: From PIE *méh₂tēr 'mother'; Latin māter and English 'mother' are cognates.

examples.original: ὁ παῖς ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ παίζει.
examples.translation: The child plays in the marketplace.
The child is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the child.

entries.etymology: The etymology is uncertain; the word covers child, slave, and dependent.

examples.translation: The king is great.
The king is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the king.

entries.etymology: The stem βασιλ- is of uncertain origin; the suffix -εύς marks an agent or role.

examples.translation: The hand is strong.
The hand is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the hand.

entries.etymology: From PIE *ǵʰésr 'hand'; Sanskrit hásta- and Albanian dorë are related.

examples.original: τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καλόν ἐστιν.
examples.translation: The name of the man is beautiful.
The name is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the name.

entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁nómn̥ 'name'; Latin nōmen and English 'name' are cognates.

examples.original: τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου θνητόν ἐστιν.
examples.translation: The body of the human being is mortal.
The body is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the body.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the word is the standard prose term for a living body.

examples.translation: The work is beautiful.
The work is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the work.

entries.etymology: From PIE *wérǵom 'work'; English 'work' and German Werk are cognates.

examples.translation: We give the gift to the child.
The gift is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the gift.

entries.etymology: From the PIE root *deh₃- 'give'; Latin dōnum and dō are cognates.

examples.translation: The day is long.
The day is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the day.

entries.etymology: Related to ἦμαρ 'day'; from PIE *h₂eh₁mer- 'day'.

examples.translation: The night is long.
The night is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the night.

entries.etymology: From PIE *nókʷts 'night'; Latin nox and English 'night' are cognates.

examples.translation: The sea is beautiful.
The sea is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the sea.

entries.etymology: Probably a Pre-Greek substrate word, like many Greek terms for landscape and sea.

examples.original: ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ὁ ἄνθρωπος μένει.
examples.translation: The man remains in the marketplace.
The marketplace is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the marketplace.

entries.etymology: From ἀγείρω 'gather'; the place where the assembly gathers.

examples.translation: The house is small.
The house is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the house.

entries.etymology: From PIE *weyḱ- 'settlement'; Latin vīcus 'village' and Sanskrit viś 'settlement' are related.

examples.translation: The people guard the laws.
The people is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the people.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the word denotes a territorial district and its people.

examples.translation: The law is just.
The law is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the law.

entries.etymology: From νέμω 'distribute, allot'; a norm is what is allotted or established.

examples.translation: The soldier is strong.
The soldier is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the soldier.

entries.etymology: From στρατός 'army' + -ιώτης, a suffix forming nouns of role or membership.

examples.original: ὁ πολίτης ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ μένει.
examples.translation: The citizen remains in the marketplace.
The citizen is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the citizen.

entries.etymology: Derived from πόλις 'city' with the suffix -ίτης.

examples.translation: Death is common.
The death is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the death.

entries.etymology: Related to θνῄσκω 'die'; the exact Indo-European reconstruction is debated.

examples.translation: Life is short.
The life is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the life.

entries.etymology: From PIE *gʷeyh₃- 'live'; Latin vīvō and English 'quick' (as 'living') are related.

examples.translation: Excellence is beautiful.
The excellence is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the excellence.

entries.etymology: Derived from the same root as ἄριστος 'best'; the noun denotes fitness or excellence.

examples.translation: I write the letter.
The letter is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the letter.

entries.etymology: From ἐπί 'to' + στέλλω 'send'; literally 'something sent to someone'.

examples.translation: Wisdom is great.
The wisdom is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the wisdom.

entries.etymology: Abstract noun from σοφός 'wise'; the adjective's own etymology is uncertain.

examples.translation: The truth is beautiful.
The truth is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the truth.

entries.etymology: From ἀ- 'not' + λήθη 'forgetting, concealment'; literally 'unconcealment'.

examples.translation: Hope is great.
The hope is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the hope.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the noun denotes expectation for good or ill.

examples.translation: Nature is wise.
The nature is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the nature.

entries.etymology: From φύω 'grow, bring forth'; the noun denotes the inherent nature of a thing.

examples.translation: The story is beautiful.
The myth is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the myth.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; in early Greek the word covers speech, report, and story.

examples.translation: The horse is swift.
The horse is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the horse.

entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁éḱwos 'horse'; Latin equus and Sanskrit áśva are cognates.

examples.translation: Justice is great.
The justice is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the justice.

entries.etymology: From the PIE root *deyḱ- 'show, point out', also reflected in Latin dīcō 'say'.

examples.translation: Time is long.
The time is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the time.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the word is already Homeric in the sense of time.

examples.translation: The grain is good.
The grain is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the grain.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the word denotes grain and, by extension, food.

examples.translation: My friend is good.
The friend is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the friend.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the same stem supplies the adjective φίλος 'dear'.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (ἀγαθός, ἀγαθή, ἀγαθόν)

examples.translation: The man is good.

examples.original: Ἀγαθός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The good man is here.
The person sees the good woman.

entries.etymology: Etymology unknown; the word is already the standard adjective for 'good' in Homer.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (καλός, καλή, καλόν)

examples.translation: The house is beautiful.

examples.original: Καλός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The beautiful man is here.
The person sees the beautiful woman.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; the adjective covers beauty, fitness, and nobility.

examples.translation: The king is great.

examples.original: Μέγας ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The great man is here.
The person sees the great woman.

irregularForms: Nominative singular uses the short stem μεγα- (μέγας, μέγα); oblique cases use μεγαλ-.
entries.etymology: From PIE *méǵh₂s 'great'; Latin magnus is a cognate.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (μικρός, μικρά, μικρόν)

examples.translation: The child is small.

examples.original: Μικρός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The small man is here.
The person sees the small woman.

entries.etymology: Often cited alongside σμικρός; the relation between the two forms is debated.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (σοφός, σοφή, σοφόν)

examples.translation: The teacher is wise.

examples.original: Σοφός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The wise man is here.
The person sees the wise woman.

entries.etymology: The adjective's etymology is uncertain; it covers practical skill as well as wisdom.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (δεινός, δεινή, δεινόν)

examples.translation: The speech is clever.

examples.original: Δεινός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The terrible man is here.
The person sees the terrible woman.

entries.etymology: From δείδω 'fear'; the sense ranges from 'fearful' to 'formidable' and 'clever'.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (δίκαιος, δικαία, δίκαιον)

examples.translation: The law is just.

examples.original: Δίκαιος ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The just man is here.
The person sees the just woman.

entries.etymology: Derived from δίκη 'justice, judgment'.

examples.translation: The grain is abundant.

examples.original: Πολύς ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The much man is here.
The person sees the much woman.

irregularForms: Nominative and accusative singular use the stem πολυ-; the other cases use πολλ-.
entries.etymology: From PIE *pl̥h₁ús 'full, much'; Latin plūs and English 'full' are related.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (νέος, νέα, νέον)

examples.translation: The house is new.

examples.original: Νέος ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The new man is here.
The person sees the new woman.

entries.etymology: From PIE *néwos 'new'; Latin novus and English 'new' are cognates.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (μακρός, μακρά, μακρόν)

examples.translation: The river is long.

examples.original: Μακρός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The long man is here.
The person sees the long woman.

entries.etymology: Probably from PIE *mh₂ḱrós 'long'; Latin macer 'lean' is sometimes compared.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (κακός, κακή, κακόν)

examples.translation: War is evil.

examples.original: Κακός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The bad man is here.
The person sees the bad woman.

entries.etymology: Etymology unknown; the adjective contrasts with ἀγαθός and καλός.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (ἰσχυρός, ἰσχυρά, ἰσχυρόν)

examples.translation: The soldier is strong.

examples.original: Ἰσχυρός ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The strong man is here.
The person sees the strong woman.

entries.etymology: Derived from ἰσχύς 'strength'.

entries.grammaticalClass: First and second declension adjective (ἐλεύθερος, ἐλευθέρα, ἐλεύθερον)

examples.translation: The citizen is free.

examples.original: Ἐλεύθερος ἄνθρωπος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The free man is here.
The person sees the free woman.

entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; perhaps a Pre-Greek word. Latin līber 'free' is not a proven cognate.

examples.translation: I speak the word.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει ὅτι ἐγώ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The person says that ἐγώ is in the marketplace.

examples.original: Εἰ ἐγώ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: If ἐγώ is in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: Enclitic forms μου, μοι, με are common alongside ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ.
entries.etymology: From PIE *éǵh₂ 'I'; Latin ego and English 'I' are cognates.

examples.translation: You guard the law.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει ὅτι σύ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The person says that σύ is in the marketplace.

examples.original: Εἰ σύ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: If σύ is in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: Enclitic forms σου, σοι, σε are common alongside σοῦ, σοί, σέ.
entries.etymology: From PIE *túh₂ 'you'; Latin tū and English 'thou' are cognates.

examples.translation: He sees the house.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει ὅτι αὐτός ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The person says that αὐτός is in the marketplace.

examples.original: Εἰ αὐτός ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: If αὐτός is in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: The pronoun has a full three-gender paradigm; the listing here shows representative forms.
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₂ew- 'again, away'; the sense 'self' develops from 'the very one'.

examples.translation: This man is wise.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει ὅτι οὗτος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The person says that οὗτος is in the marketplace.

examples.original: Εἰ οὗτος ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐστίν, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: If οὗτος is in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: The paradigm combines the stem τοῦτ-/ταύτ- with the definite article in the nominative.
entries.etymology: A compound demonstrative; the initial element is related to the ancient *so-/*to- demonstrative stem.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λύει ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person looses in the marketplace.

examples.original: Τότε ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἔλυεν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Then the person loosed in the marketplace.

examples.original: Αὔριον ἐγώ λύσω ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will loose in the marketplace.

entries.etymology: From the PIE root *lewh₁- 'loosen, cut off'; Latin luō is sometimes compared.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος γράφει ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person writes in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ ἔγραψα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I writed in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ γέγραφα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I writed in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

entries.etymology: The verb originally meant 'scratch, engrave'; the further etymology is uncertain.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person says in the marketplace.

examples.original: Τότε ἐγώ ἔλεγον ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Then I sayed in the marketplace.

examples.original: Αὔριον ἐγώ λέξω ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will say in the marketplace.

irregularForms: The aorist εἶπον is suppletive and far more common than ἔλεξα.
entries.etymology: From PIE *leǵ- 'gather, speak'; Latin legō 'gather, read' is a cognate.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἔχει ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person haves in the marketplace.

examples.original: Τότε ἐγώ εἶχον ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Then I haved in the marketplace.

examples.original: Αὔριον ἐγώ ἕξω ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will have in the marketplace.

irregularForms: The future and aorist stems are ἑξ- and σχ-, not built on the present stem ἐχ-.
entries.etymology: From PIE *seǵʰ- 'hold, possess'; Sanskrit sáhate and Gothic sigis are related.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ποιεῖ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person makes in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ ἐποίησα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I maked in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ πεποίηκα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I maked in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: Contract verb: the present stem ποιε- contracts with the endings (ποιέ-ω → ποιῶ).
entries.etymology: From PIE *kʷey- 'arrange, make'; the exact cognate set is debated.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁρᾷ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person sees in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ εἶδον ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I seed in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ ἑώρακα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I seed in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

irregularForms: The aorist εἶδον and future ὄψομαι are suppletive.
entries.etymology: The etymology is uncertain; the verb is suppleted in several tenses.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀκούει ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person hears in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ ἤκουσα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I heared in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ἐγώ ἀκήκοα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because I heared in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

entries.etymology: The etymology is uncertain; the verb takes the genitive or accusative of the thing heard.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος φησίν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person asserts in the marketplace.

examples.original: Τότε ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἔφη ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Then the person asserted in the marketplace.
I assert in the marketplace.

irregularForms: Defective verb: the present system and imperfect are the forms in ordinary use.
entries.etymology: From PIE *bʰéh₂ti 'speaks'; Latin fārī 'speak' is related.

examples.original: Ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐστίν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: The person bes in the marketplace.

examples.original: Τότε ἐγώ ἦν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Then I bed in the marketplace.

examples.original: Αὔριον ἐγώ ἔσομαι ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will be in the marketplace.

irregularForms: Enclitic present forms (εἰμι, ἐστι, ἐσμεν, ἐστε, εἰσι) occur without the movable nu.
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁ésmi 'I am'; Latin sum and English 'is' are cognates.

examples.translation: You do well.

examples.original: Ἡ λέξις «εὖ» ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The word “εὖ” is in the book.

examples.original: Περὶ τῆς λέξεως «εὖ» ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει.
examples.translation: The person speaks about the word “εὖ”.

entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁su- 'good, well'; Sanskrit su- 'well' is a cognate.

examples.translation: Now I see the house.

examples.original: Ἡ λέξις «νῦν» ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The word “νῦν” is in the book.

examples.original: Περὶ τῆς λέξεως «νῦν» ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει.
examples.translation: The person speaks about the word “νῦν”.

entries.etymology: From PIE *nú 'now'; Latin nunc and English 'now' are cognates.

examples.translation: We remain in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἡ λέξις «ἐν» ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The word “ἐν” is in the book.

examples.original: Περὶ τῆς λέξεως «ἐν» ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει.
examples.translation: The person speaks about the word “ἐν”.

entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁en 'in'; Latin in and English 'in' are cognates.

examples.original: ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ μένουσιν.
examples.translation: The father and the mother remain in the house.

examples.original: Ἡ λέξις «καί» ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ ἐστίν.
examples.translation: The word “καί” is in the book.

examples.original: Περὶ τῆς λέξεως «καί» ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει.
examples.translation: The person speaks about the word “καί”.

entries.etymology: The further etymology is uncertain; the word is already the ordinary copulative in Homer.

The person sees a part of the messenger.
The person sees the messenger.

examples.translation: The person leads in the marketplace.

examples.original: Ἐπεὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἤγαγεν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἡ γυνὴ χαίρει.
examples.translation: Because the person leaded in the marketplace, the woman rejoices.

examples.original: Ὁ οἶκος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἤχθη.
examples.translation: The house is leaded by the person.

entries.sourceReference: Wilfred E. Major, CPL Online 4 (2008), 80% list

examples.translation: The contest is in the marketplace.
The person sees a part of the contest.
The person sees the contest.

entries.sourceReference: Wilfred E. Major, CPL Online 4 (2008), 80% list

examples.translation: The sister is in the marketplace.
